Chapter 4: Letting Go of the Need for Control
Have you ever noticed how natural it feels to want to steer everything in your life? Most of us set goals, make plans, and try to shape outcomes—almost as if, with enough effort, we could guarantee the future turns out exactly as we hope.
There’s a certain comfort in believing that control equals security. But, as you’ve probably experienced, life rarely follows even the best-laid plans.
Picture someone laser-focused on hitting a big career milestone. They map out every move, track every deadline, and measure progress down to the last detail. But what happens when things go sideways? Maybe a project falls apart, or that long-awaited promotion gets pushed back. Suddenly, their sense of control starts slipping away. Frustration creeps in. Doubts get louder. And the harder they try to force things back on track, the more out of reach success seems.
Sound familiar? This need for control is something almost everyone wrestles with, and honestly, it often leads to more stress instead of less. It’s kind of wild—sometimes, the tighter we cling to our plans, the more painful it is when life doesn’t play along.
Here’s something to pay attention to: a lot of our suffering comes from the gap between what we expect and what actually happens.
But what if there’s another way to handle life’s unpredictability?
Some philosophies suggest a different path. Instead of obsessively trying to control every outcome, they invite us to let go a little—to accept that life is unpredictable, and outcomes won’t always be in our hands.
Now, this isn’t about giving up or being passive. It’s about seeing where our influence really lies, and focusing our energy there.
Let me give you a real-world example. A close friend of mine was diagnosed with a chronic illness. For months, they poured everything into finding answers: researching treatments, chasing second opinions, following every bit of advice—hoping, deep down, to regain control over their body. But progress was slow. Setbacks kept coming. Eventually, they realized something had to shift.
Instead of trying to force their health back to what it was, they turned their focus to managing their response. They learned to adapt, to find small joys in each day, and to accept the uncertainty that came with their condition. Life didn’t suddenly get easier, but it did become more bearable.
That shift—letting go of the need for control—can be truly transformative. Suddenly, there’s more room for flexibility and resilience. Setbacks don’t sting quite so much, and sometimes, unexpected opportunities pop up that you wouldn’t have noticed before.
Most of us don’t realize just how much energy goes into trying to force life into a specific shape. But when you finally loosen that grip, there’s a new sense of freedom. The world feels a little less threatening, and the future doesn’t seem quite so intimidating.
Letting go of control doesn’t mean you have to abandon your goals or dreams. It simply means holding them a bit more lightly, and being willing to adapt when things change. Trust that you’ll be able to handle whatever comes, rather than insisting everything has to go your way.
